## Why RAG exists

Ask a large language model something like "What were the key discussion
points in our company's board meeting yesterday?" and it will do one of three
things: hallucinate a confident but false answer, admit it doesn't know
(because its training data has a cutoff date), or give a generic non-answer
("board meetings typically discuss strategy and finances…"). None of those
are useful, and all three come from the same root causes: the model's
knowledge is **static** (frozen at training time), it has **no memory of your
private data** (it never saw your internal documents), and it is **prone to
hallucination** (when unsure, it guesses plausibly instead of admitting
ignorance).

**Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** retrieves relevant documents from an
external knowledge source — usually a vector database — and injects them into
the LLM's prompt, so the model generates an answer grounded in real,
retrieved data rather than in memory alone. It's the difference between an
open-book and a closed-book exam: without RAG, the model answers purely from
memory and may hallucinate; with RAG, it looks the answer up first, then
answers from what it found. Embeddings and similarity search — covered in
[Vector Databases and Embeddings](01_vector_databases_and_embeddings.qmd) —
are the fuel and the engine; RAG is the complete vehicle built around them.

Every RAG pipeline runs in three phases: **retrieve** relevant documents
using similarity search, **augment** the prompt with those documents, and
**generate** an answer grounded in that context.

## The complete RAG architecture

The full pipeline splits into two steps that run at very different times:
**indexing**, done once offline, and **querying**, done every time a user
asks something.

```{mermaid}
graph TD
    A["Documents<br>(PDFs, wikis, emails, code)"] --> B["Chunking<br>(split into passages)"]
    B --> C["Embedding<br>(chunk → vector)"]
    C --> D[("Vector DB<br>(chunk + vector + metadata)")]
```

### Phase one: indexing (preparation)

This is the offline step — building the "textbook" the system will later
search:

| Step | Action | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Load | Collect all source documents | Company policies, product manuals, support tickets |
| 2. Chunk | Split into semantic units | Each chunk = 512 tokens with 50-token overlap |
| 3. Embed | Generate a vector for each chunk | `chunk_vector = embedding_model(chunk_text)` |
| 4. Store | Save chunk + vector + metadata | `{id: 123, text: "...", vector: [0.1, 0.9, ...], source: "HR_policy.pdf"}` |

### Phase two: querying (inference)

This runs on every user question. For the query "What is our vacation
policy?": embed the query, run similarity search against the vector database
to get the top-*k* nearest chunks (e.g., `k=5`), retrieve the actual text of
those chunks, build a prompt containing system instructions plus the
retrieved chunks plus the user's question, send it to the LLM, and return the
generated answer — e.g., "Our vacation policy provides 15 days per year…"

## Three RAG architecture patterns

| Pattern | Flow | Pros | Cons | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Naive RAG | Query → Retrieve → Augment → Generate → Answer | Easy to build, works for simple Q&A | No quality checks; retrieves wrong chunks often | Prototypes, internal demos |
| 2. Advanced RAG | Query → rewrite → Retrieve → Rerank → Filter → Augment → Generate | Much higher accuracy | More latency, more components to maintain | Production systems |
| 3. Modular / Agentic RAG | System decides which retriever to call (vector DB, web search, SQL, API); can retrieve iteratively | Most powerful — answers complex multi-hop questions | Complex to build and debug | Multi-hop, tool-using assistants |

Advanced RAG adds two things around the naive loop: **pre-retrieval**
processing (rewriting an ambiguous query, expanding it with synonyms) and
**post-retrieval** processing (reranking chunks with a more expensive
cross-encoder, filtering out low-quality ones). Modular/agentic RAG goes
further still — the system can ask a follow-up question, retrieve again, and
chain retrievals together, which is the only way to answer something like
"What is the capital of the country where Einstein was born?" (a single
retrieval can't connect those two facts).

## Walking through a real query

User asks: *"How many vacation days do new hires get?"*

1. **Embed the query** → `[0.23, -0.56, 0.78, ...]`
2. **Similarity search** returns the top 3 chunks: Chunk A (score 0.92,
   "New hires in their first year receive 10 vacation days"), Chunk B (score
   0.88, "Employees with 1–5 years of service receive 15 days"), Chunk C
   (score 0.45, "Vacation policy was revised in January 2024").
3. **Reranking** (optional): a cross-encoder re-evaluates all three and
   promotes Chunk A to rank 1, dropping Chunk C entirely as irrelevant noise.
4. **Build the prompt**: `Context: New hires in their first year receive 10
   vacation days. Question: How many vacation days do new hires get? Answer:`
5. **LLM generation**: "New hires receive 10 vacation days during their
   first year of employment."
6. **Return to user.**

Notice what happened: the LLM did not "know" this fact. It read it from the
retrieved chunk and paraphrased it — that's the entire point of RAG.

### Where basic RAG breaks

| Problem | Explanation | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Low recall | Relevant chunks not retrieved | Improve chunking, embedding model, or increase *k* |
| Low precision | Irrelevant chunks retrieved | Add reranking, metadata filtering |
| Context window overflow | Retrieved too much text | Compress chunks, use a smaller *k* |
| Outdated data | Vector DB hasn't been updated | Implement incremental indexing |
| Multi-hop questions | Single retrieval can't connect separate facts | Use iterative or agentic RAG |

## Chunking strategies

Imagine splitting a 10-page medical paper into rigid 100-character chunks.
One chunk ends with "The patient showed no signs of" and the next begins
with "improvement after treatment." A user asks "Did the patient improve?"
and the system retrieves one chunk with no answer, or the other with missing
context — either way, a wrong answer. **Chunking is the art of breaking
documents into pieces that are meaningful, self-contained, and searchable.**

Good chunking has three goals: **semantic completeness** (each chunk should
make sense on its own — cutting a sentence in half fails this), **appropriate
size** (small enough for efficient retrieval, large enough to hold context —
50-character chunks lose meaning, 5000-character chunks waste the context
window), and **contextual boundaries** (respect the document's natural
structure — never split inside a table, code block, or list). The golden
rule: a chunk should be a unit of meaning — a paragraph, a function — not an
arbitrary slice of bytes.

| Strategy | How it works | Best for | Avoid for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed-size | Splits every *N* characters/tokens, regardless of content | Logs, uniform text, unknown structure | Any structured document — it breaks sentences and ideas |
| Sentence-based | Splits on punctuation boundaries | Conversational text, support tickets | Very long or complex sentences; abbreviations like "Dr. Smith" can fool it |
| Recursive / hierarchical | Recursively splits by decreasing boundary — document → section → paragraph → sentence — stopping once a chunk is within the target size | Books, manuals, legal documents with clear headings | Flat, unstructured text with no real hierarchy |
| Semantic | Embeds sliding windows of sentences; splits where similarity between adjacent windows drops sharply | Large, mixed-content documents — textbooks, research papers | Small or simple documents — computationally overkill |

**Fixed-size**, concretely: splitting `"The quick brown fox jumps over the
lazy dog. The dog barks."` at a rigid 15 characters produces `"The quick
brown"`, `" fox jumps ove"`, `"r the lazy dog."`, `" The dog barks."` — note
the second and third chunks each cut a word in half. It's trivial to
implement and gives predictable, uniform chunk sizes (a typical parameter
choice is 512 tokens with 50 tokens of overlap), which is exactly why it
works fine for homogeneous text like news articles or log files — but
overlap only patches the symptom, it doesn't fix the underlying loss of
semantic boundaries.

**Sentence-based**, concretely: `"The quick brown fox jumps. The lazy dog
sleeps. The cat watches."` splits cleanly into three chunks, one per
sentence. This is easy to implement with NLP libraries like NLTK or spaCy
and preserves grammatical units, but individual sentences can be too short to
carry context on their own, and naive splitting has no protection against
breaking on a period inside an abbreviation like "Dr. Smith."

**Recursive / hierarchical**, concretely: the splitter first checks whether
the whole document fits the target size; if not, it descends one level and
retries on each piece, e.g.:

```
Document
  ├── Section 1 (too large)
  │     ├── Paragraph 1 (good size) → keep
  │     └── Paragraph 2 (still too large)
  │           ├── Sentence 1 → keep
  │           └── Sentence 2 → keep
  └── Section 2 (good size) → keep
```

Recursive chunking keeps a paragraph attached to its section, and a sentence
to its paragraph, so the system can store parent-child relationships — but it
requires actually parsing the document's headings. A related, simpler variant
— **recursive character chunking** — looks for structural markers in order
(paragraph breaks `\n\n`, then sentence-ending punctuation, then whitespace)
and splits at the highest-priority marker that keeps chunks near the target
size; it respects natural text boundaries well for markdown files, blog
posts, and essays, but can still separate a chart or table from the
paragraph that explains it.

**Semantic** is the most content-aware of the four: it detects where meaning
shifts by comparing the embeddings of consecutive sentence windows, splitting
only where similarity drops. Concretely, over five sentences `S1..S5`, embed
each 3-sentence sliding window — Window A = `(S1,S2,S3)` → vector `V1`,
Window B = `(S2,S3,S4)` → vector `V2`, Window C = `(S3,S4,S5)` → vector `V3`
— and if `similarity(V1, V2)` stays high but `similarity(V2, V3)` drops
sharply, that's a topic shift, so the chunker splits between `S3` and `S4`.
This finds natural topic boundaries that structural splitting can't see, at
the cost of running an embedding model during indexing, not just at query
time.

### Chunk overlap

Regardless of strategy, chunks should almost always overlap — chunk 2
repeats the last few tokens of chunk 1:

```
Chunk 1: [A B C D E F G]
Chunk 2: [F G H I J K L]   ← overlaps by 2 tokens (F, G)
Chunk 3: [K L M N O P Q]   ← overlaps by 2 tokens (K, L)
```

Without overlap, "The patient showed no" ends one chunk and "signs of
improvement" starts the next, and the LLM never sees the complete sentence.
With overlap, both chunks contain the boundary. Recommended overlap is
10–20% of chunk size: 512-token chunks get 50–100 tokens of overlap;
256-token chunks get 25–50.

## Hybrid search and Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Pure vector search misses exact keyword matches — a query for "GPT-4" can
retrieve documents about "a language model" instead of the literal string.
Pure BM25 (keyword search) misses semantic meaning entirely — "canine
therapy" doesn't match "dog treatment" at all if no words overlap.

**Hybrid search** runs both a vector ANN search and a BM25 keyword search in
parallel, then merges the two result lists with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion
(RRF)**:

$$\text{RRF score} = \sum_{\text{list}} \frac{1}{k + \text{rank}_i}, \quad k = 60$$

RRF rewards a document that ranks highly in *both* lists, without needing any
weights tuned by hand — and empirically it outperforms a weighted linear
combination of the two scores in most benchmarks. Most modern vector
databases (Weaviate, Elasticsearch, Qdrant) expose hybrid search natively.

## Cross-encoder reranking — the second precision gate

A **bi-encoder** (the retrieval stage) embeds the query and each document
independently — fast, but it can miss subtle relevance because query and
document never actually interact during scoring. A **cross-encoder**
(reranking stage) takes the `(query, document)` pair *jointly* and scores
them together — far more accurate, because it can model the interaction
between query tokens and document tokens directly, at the cost of one
inference call per candidate (O(n), versus O(1) for bi-encoder similarity).

The standard workflow: retrieve the top 50 candidates cheaply with the
bi-encoder, rerank those 50 with the cross-encoder, then pass only the top 3
to 5 to the LLM. Rerank only when retrieval returns more than ~10 candidates
— it adds roughly 50–200ms of latency per query. Common models:
`ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` (fast), `bge-reranker-large` (more accurate), or a
hosted option like the Cohere Rerank API.

## RAG evaluation — the triad you must measure

You cannot guess whether an architecture change improved retrieval — you
have to measure it:

- **Context Precision** — are the retrieved chunks actually relevant? (no
  noise)
- **Context Recall** — did retrieval find *all* the chunks needed to answer?
  (completeness)
- **Answer Faithfulness** — does the generated answer stick to the retrieved
  context, or does it add facts that weren't there? (hallucination risk)
- **Answer Relevance** — does the answer actually address what the user
  asked?

**RAGAS** is the standard open-source framework: it computes all four
metrics automatically using an LLM as judge. A useful alert rule: if
faithfulness drops below 0.85, the retrieval or the prompt has regressed and
needs attention.

## Building production-ready RAG pipelines

Turning a working prototype into something stable and accurate at scale
means implementing five layers:

```
[Ingestion Layer] → [Hybrid Retrieval] → [Two-Stage Reranking] → [Data Sync / CDC] → [Evaluation Triad]
```

1. **The ingestion layer.** Production data is rarely clean markdown — it's
   multi-column PDFs, scanned documents, and messy financial tables. Modern
   pipelines use vision-based layout parsers (Docling, Unstructured) to
   convert these into clean semantic trees that preserve table structure.
   Every chunk should also be stamped with metadata — `file_id`,
   `security_clearance_level`, `creation_date`, `document_version` — you
   can't just inject raw text.
2. **Hybrid retrieval.** Relying only on vector search is a classic prototype
   mistake — it struggles with exact product serial numbers, code symbols,
   or jargon. Combine dense (vector) retrieval with sparse (BM25) retrieval
   via RRF, as covered above.
3. **Two-stage reranking**, to mitigate "lost-in-the-middle": dumping the top
   30 raw chunks into an LLM overwhelms it and it starts ignoring
   information buried in the middle of the prompt. Stage one fetches the
   top 50 candidates cheaply; stage two reranks with a cross-encoder and
   keeps only the best 3–5.
4. **Keeping data fresh — incremental sync and CDC.** A production knowledge
   base isn't static; a nightly full wipe-and-reindex doesn't scale.

   | Sync strategy | How it works | When to use it |
   |---|---|---|
   | Incremental updates | Monitors folder timestamps or commit histories, re-indexes only new/modified documents | Standard corporate files and wikis |
   | Change Data Capture (CDC) | Hooks directly into a live database to mirror inserts/updates/deletes into the vector store instantly | Highly dynamic data — live inventory, ticketing |
5. **Continuous evaluation.** Score every architectural change against the
   RAG triad (context relevance, groundedness, answer relevance) — you
   cannot tell whether a change helped without measuring it.

## Lab: building an advanced RAG system

The [Day 3 lab notebook](Day3_Lab.ipynb) implements this entire pipeline end
to end over a small built-in knowledge base of data-engineering documents
(Kafka, Delta Lake, RAG, HNSW, hybrid search): document chunking, a ChromaDB
vector index (HNSW backend), BM25 keyword search, RRF hybrid fusion,
cross-encoder reranking, RAG prompt construction, and RAGAS-style precision
and similarity evaluation — all on a real, executed run using local,
free components (no hosted vector DB, no paid embeddings API, no GPU).

What to look for in the output:

- Candidate counts moving through each stage — vector search, BM25 search,
  RRF fusion — for four different queries against the same eight-document
  knowledge base.
- The cross-encoder reranking step narrowing the fused candidates down to
  the top 3, with each surviving chunk's text printed.
- The final RAG prompt assembled from the top reranked chunks, plus the
  retrieval metrics (`context_precision`, `avg_similarity`) and a pass/fail
  quality read-out, printed for every query.
